en.title: Demography and Social Statistics: the whole course
en.short: What demography and social statistics is, how the degree is organised, its main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Demography is the study of human populations: how many people there are, how they are composed by age, sex and other characteristics, where they live, and how births, deaths and migration change them. Social statistics is the wider craft of measuring social conditions with numbers, from literacy to employment to health.

This course joins the two. It teaches the concepts and measures demographers use, the mathematics and statistics those measures need, the sources the data come from, and the analysis of fertility, mortality, migration, households, ageing, health, urbanisation and policy.

The aim is practical: to read a population figure, know how it was produced, and judge whether it is sound.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook for the exact structure.

In Nigeria, a BSc in Demography and Social Statistics is commonly a four-year programme, following benchmarks set by the National Universities Commission. Polytechnics, under the National Board for Technical Education, award the ND and HND in statistics and related fields, and some colleges of education award the NCE. A master’s degree usually takes one to two years and ends with a dissertation.

In the United Kingdom a first degree is usually three years; in South Africa, three or four. In all cases the pattern is similar: foundations first, core demographic methods in the middle, and a supervised project or dissertation at the end.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The course begins with foundations. You meet population studies and demography as fields, then the basic concepts and measures: rates, ratios, proportions and the balancing equation. Mathematics for demography covers the algebra and the exponential and logistic growth you will need. Statistics for demography covers description, probability and inference.

Next come the sources of data: the census, vital registration and vital statistics, and sample surveys, with their strengths and their errors. Population composition, and population growth and components of change, then show how the pieces fit together.

The core follows: fertility, mortality, life tables, migration, nuptiality and households, estimates and projections, demographic transition and theory, population and development, policy and programmes, family planning and reproductive health, health demography, urbanisation, ageing, social statistics and indicators, data analysis, and research design and ethics, ending in a project.

At master’s level the course turns to advanced demographic methods, event history and survival analysis, causal inference and programme evaluation, and a research seminar leading to a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Demography is learned by calculating. After reading a formula, close the book and compute a rate from raw numbers, then check the units. Keep one sheet of definitions and formulas and add to it weekly.

Work with real data. Take a census table or a survey report from your own country’s statistics office and compute an age distribution or a crude death rate. Note the year and the definition of every figure.

Learn one statistical package, such as R, Stata or SPSS, early. Read each method with its assumptions in mind; a rate is only as good as the population count underneath it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
The commonest error is to confuse a rate, a ratio and a proportion. A rate has a time dimension; a proportion does not. Students also forget to use a mid-year population, or multiply by 1,000 in one place and not another.

A second error is to trust data without asking how they were collected. Census undercounts and incomplete birth registration are normal, and they change the answer.

A third is to treat correlation as causation, or a projection as a forecast. A fourth is to compare figures across countries without checking definitions and dates. Always state the source, the year and the denominator.

keyPoints: Demography studies the size, composition and change of populations through births, deaths and migration.
Social statistics supplies the measurement tools that demographic work depends on.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Every rate needs a stated denominator, a stated period and a stated source.
Learn by computing from real data, not by memorising formulas alone.
Correlation is not causation, and a projection is not a forecast.

en.title: Population Studies and Demography
en.short: Defines demography and population studies, their scope, links to other fields, and components of change.

sections.heading: Definitions and scope
sections.text:
Demography is the scientific study of human populations: their size, distribution and composition, and how these change through births, deaths and migration. Population studies is broader. It examines populations in relation to social, economic, cultural and political life.

Some writers use the two terms interchangeably; others treat demography as the technical core and population studies as the wider field. Formal demography concentrates on the components of change and their measurement. Social demography links population to society, institutions and policy.

sections.heading: Links to other fields
sections.text:
Sociology studies family, migration, inequality and ageing, all shaped by population. Economics studies labour supply, dependency, consumption and savings; population size and age structure affect these.

Statistics supplies data collection, sampling and inference. Public health uses population data to plan services and study disease and death. These links make demography interdisciplinary.

sections.heading: Components of change
sections.text:
A population changes through three components. Births add people; deaths remove people; migration moves people across a boundary. Immigration is entry and emigration is exit; net migration is immigration minus emigration. Natural increase is births minus deaths.

A concrete case: Amina, a community health worker in a fictional town, sees more births in one ward, young adults leaving for the city, and older residents dying. Each observation points to a component; together they explain local change.

sections.heading: Why the distinction matters
sections.text:
The distinction matters in practice. A government may ask a demographer to describe a population and a population-studies scholar to explain why it is changing and what that means for schools, jobs or health care.

The first task is mainly technical; the second draws on several disciplines. Both need reliable data, and both must be clear about definitions.

keyPoints: Demography studies the size, distribution, composition and change of human populations.
Population studies is broader and links population to social, economic, cultural and political life.
Formal demography is the technical core; social demography is interdisciplinary.
The three components of population change are births, deaths and migration.
Net migration is immigration minus emigration, and natural increase is births minus deaths.
Sociology, economics, statistics and public health all contribute to population studies.

en.title: Demographic Concepts and Measures
en.short: Rates, ratios, proportions, crude and specific rates, cohort and period measures, stocks, flows and balancing equation.

sections.heading: Rates, ratios and proportions
sections.text: A proportion is a part divided by the whole; it lies between 0 and 1 and can be written as a percentage. A ratio compares two quantities, often written a:b, and need not sum to one. A rate measures events per unit of exposure in a stated time. The denominator must match the numerator in time and population. A crude rate uses the whole population; a specific rate uses a subgroup, such as women aged 15 to 19. Crude rates are easy but can be distorted by age structure, so compare specific rates or standardise (adjust to a common age structure) before concluding.

sections.heading: Cohort, period, stock and flow
sections.text: A cohort measure follows the same people over time, for example the fertility of women born in 2000. A period measure mixes events in one calendar year across all ages, so it is affected by timing. A stock is a count at a moment, such as population on census night. A flow is a count over an interval, such as births in a year. Person-years are the total time people spend alive in a population during an interval; one person observed for one year contributes one person-year. Rates with person-years in the denominator are incidence rates.

sections.heading: Worked example and balancing equation
sections.text: Suppose a district has a mid-year population of 50,000 and 1,500 births in the year. Crude birth rate = 1,500 ÷ 50,000 × 1,000 = 30 per 1,000. If women aged 15 to 19 contributed 4,000 person-years and had 120 births, their age-specific fertility rate = 120 ÷ 4,000 × 1,000 = 30 per 1,000. The same number here is a coincidence; the specific rate uses only that age group. The balancing equation: P1 = P0 + B − D + I − O, where B births, D deaths, I in-migrants, O out-migrants. If P0 = 100,000, B = 3,000, D = 1,200, I = 500, O = 300, then P1 = 102,000. Check: 100,000 + 3,000 − 1,200 + 500 − 300 = 102,000.

keyPoints: A proportion is a part over the whole; a ratio compares two quantities; a rate relates events to exposure in a stated time.
Crude rates use the whole population, while specific rates use a subgroup and are less distorted by age structure.
A cohort measure follows the same people over time; a period measure uses events in one calendar year across all ages.
A stock is measured at a moment; a flow is measured over an interval, and person-years measure exposure time.
Crude birth rate = births ÷ mid-year population × 1,000; age-specific fertility rate = births to women aged x ÷ person-years of women aged x × 1,000.
Balancing equation: P1 = P0 + B − D + I − O.

en.title: Mathematics for Demography
en.short: Exponents, logs, growth rates, doubling time, exponential and logistic growth, interpolation and formula rearrangement.

sections.heading: Powers, logs and formulas
sections.text:
An exponent shows repeated multiplication: (1 + r)^t is the growth factor after t years. A logarithm gives the power needed: log base b of x is the power to which b must be raised to give x. Natural logs use base e ≈ 2.71828. Exponents and logs are inverse operations.

Because ln(a^t) = t ln a, logs let you rearrange P_t = P_0(1 + r)^t. Then r = (P_t/P_0)^(1/t) − 1 and t = ln(P_t/P_0) ÷ ln(1 + r). Use r as a decimal; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

sections.heading: Growth and doubling
sections.text:
A growth rate compares totals: r = (P_t/P_0)^(1/t) − 1. Doubling time is exactly t_d = ln 2 ÷ ln(1 + r), and roughly 70 ÷ (100r), where 100r is the percentage rate. The rule of 70 is an approximation; use exact logs for precision.

Exponential growth assumes a constant rate: P_t = P_0 e^{rt} continuously, or P_t = P_0(1 + r)^t yearly. Logistic growth adds a carrying capacity K: dP/dt = rP(1 − P/K), with solution P_t = K ÷ (1 + ((K − P_0)/P_0)e^{−rt}). Growth is fastest at K/2. Example: 1,000 people at 2% yearly for 10 years gives 1,000(1.02)^10 = 1,218.99, about 1,219, and doubling time ln 2 ÷ ln 1.02 ≈ 35.0 years.

sections.heading: Interpolation and checking
sections.text:
Linear interpolation estimates between two known points: y = y_1 + (x − x_1)/(x_2 − x_1) × (y_2 − y_1). If a district had 800,000 people in 2000 and 1,000,000 in 2010, the 2005 estimate is 800,000 + (5/10)(200,000) = 900,000.

This assumes steady change between the points, so treat it as a rough estimate. Interpolation is not projection; it does not forecast beyond the known points. Always check units, keep rates as decimals in formulas, and state whether growth is yearly or continuous.

keyPoints: P_t = P_0(1 + r)^t gives yearly compound growth; P_t = P_0 e^{rt} gives continuous growth.
r = (P_t/P_0)^(1/t) − 1 finds the average yearly growth rate from two totals.
Doubling time is t_d = ln 2 ÷ ln(1 + r), approximated by 70 ÷ (100r).
Logistic growth follows dP/dt = rP(1 − P/K), with carrying capacity K and fastest growth at K/2.
Linear interpolation is y = y_1 + (x − x_1)/(x_2 − x_1) × (y_2 − y_1).
Keep rates as decimals in formulas and multiply by 100 only to report a percentage.

en.title: Statistics for Demography
en.short: Descriptive statistics, distributions, sampling, confidence intervals, tests, correlation, regression for demography.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise a demographic variable such as household size or age at first birth. The mean is the sum divided by n. The median is the middle value when ordered. The standard deviation s measures spread around the mean. A histogram shows shape. Demographic data are often skewed, so report median and mean. For a binary variable such as contraceptive use, the proportion p is the mean of 0/1 values.

sections.heading: Probability and sampling
sections.text: A probability distribution gives the chance of each value. The binomial distribution counts successes in n independent trials with the same chance of success each time, such as boys among births. The Poisson distribution counts rare events in a fixed time or area, such as deaths in a small district. The normal distribution describes many large-sample statistics. A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic, like a sample mean, over repeated samples. Its standard deviation is the standard error. For a mean, SE = s ÷ √n.

sections.heading: Confidence and tests
sections.text: A confidence interval gives a range likely to contain the population value. For a large-sample mean, 95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SE. Example: n = 100, mean = 24.0 years, s = 5.0. SE = 5.0 ÷ √100 = 0.5. CI = 24.0 ± 1.96 × 0.5 = 23.02 to 24.98 years. A hypothesis test asks whether data are consistent with a null hypothesis, often no difference. The p-value is the chance of results at least as extreme if the null is true. Small p is evidence against the null, but does not prove it false.

sections.heading: Correlation and regression
sections.text: Correlation r measures the strength and direction of a straight-line association, from −1 to +1. Example: r = −0.4 between mother’s education and child mortality risk suggests a moderate negative association. Correlation does not prove cause. Simple regression fits y = a + bx. The slope b is the predicted change in y for a one-unit rise in x. Demographic regression can relate fertility to education, but control for age and income.

keyPoints: Mean = Σx ÷ n; standard deviation s measures spread.
Standard error of a sample mean: SE = s ÷ √n.
95% confidence interval for a large-sample mean: mean ± 1.96 × SE.
A p-value is the chance of results at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis is true.
Correlation r runs from −1 to +1 and measures straight-line association, not causation.
Simple regression y = a + bx predicts y; slope b is the change in y per one-unit change in x.

en.title: Sources of Demographic Data
en.short: Comparing censuses, civil registration, surveys and administrative records: strengths, limits and complementarity.

sections.heading: Four main sources
sections.text: Demographic data describe births, deaths, migration, age and sex. A census counts a whole population at one time, usually every ten years, though intervals vary by country. Civil registration is the continuous legal recording of births, deaths and marriages by a government office. A sample survey collects data from a selected subset and generalises to the population. Administrative records are data produced by services such as hospitals, schools, tax offices and migration authorities.

sections.heading: Strengths and limits
sections.text: Censuses give complete coverage, small-area counts and the denominators that other sources need. They are costly, infrequent and prone to omission, duplication and age misreporting. Civil registration gives continuous, legally recognised events and local detail, but it is incomplete where most births and deaths are not registered. Surveys allow detailed questions, quality control and quick results, but they carry sampling error and non-response and may not represent small areas. Administrative records are cheap and continuous, yet they cover only people who use a service and use definitions that may not match demographic concepts.

sections.heading: Coverage problems
sections.text: Coverage means who should be counted and who actually is. Every source faces gaps: people missed, events unregistered, records duplicated, boundaries changed, or definitions altered. A census may miss nomadic people or informal settlements. Registration may miss home births. A survey may miss people without a fixed address. Administrative records may count visits rather than people. Data users should ask who is included, when data were collected and whether the definitions match.

sections.heading: Working together
sections.text: Sources complement one another. A census supplies denominators and a sampling frame; a survey supplies detailed fertility or health data; registration supplies continuous events; administrative records supply service information. In a hypothetical case, Amina, a district health planner in Kano, Nigeria, wants birth estimates. Civil registration is incomplete, so she uses census counts for the population denominator, a recent survey for fertility rates and clinic records for service use. No single source is enough, and each number should be checked against another.

keyPoints: A census counts the whole population at one time and provides denominators and sampling frames, but it is costly and infrequent.
Civil registration records births, deaths and marriages continuously, but it is only reliable where registration coverage is high.
Sample surveys give detailed data from a subset, but they carry sampling error and non-response.
Administrative records are cheap and continuous, but they cover only service users and may use non-demographic definitions.
Coverage problems include omission, duplication, missing events, boundary changes and definition differences.
The sources complement one another: census for denominators, survey for detail, registration for events, records for services.

en.title: The Census: Counting a Whole Population
en.short: Purposes, planning, de facto and de jure counts, questionnaires, errors and post-enumeration checks.

sections.heading: What a census is for
sections.text:
A census is the complete count of all people in a defined area at a stated time, recording selected characteristics such as age, sex and household. Its purposes are to provide population totals and small-area data for planning, research and monitoring, and to supply the denominators for rates. The legal basis and exact questions differ by country, so always check the national census law and official reports.

A census aims to reach everyone, including people in institutions and remote areas.

sections.heading: Planning and enumeration
sections.text:
Planning starts years before enumeration: legal authority, budget, maps, questionnaire design, pilot tests, recruitment, training and publicity. Two enumeration methods are common. A de facto count records people where they are on census night, which is simple but can double-count travellers. A de jure count records people at their usual residence, which gives stable local figures but risks omission of movers. Many countries use a de facto count with a usual-residence question.

The questionnaire is usually a household schedule plus individual questions. It must be translated, pre-tested and kept short enough to complete accurately.

sections.heading: Errors and checks
sections.text:
Coverage errors mean people are missed or counted twice, causing undercount or overcount. Content errors mean the recorded characteristics are wrong, for example a wrong age or sex. Both bias planning.

A post-enumeration survey (PES) re-interviews a sample soon after the census and compares answers. It estimates coverage and content error. For example, if a PES estimates 100 people in an area but the census counted 98, net coverage is 98 ÷ 100 = 98%, a 2% undercount.

sections.heading: Use in planning
sections.text: Census data guide public planning: where to build schools, clinics and roads, how to allocate funds, and how to monitor policies. They also provide denominators for fertility and mortality rates. Because figures become out of date, planners use projections between censuses.

keyPoints: A census counts everyone in a defined area at a stated time and records selected characteristics.
De facto counts people where they are on census night; de jure counts them at their usual residence.
Planning covers legal authority, mapping, questionnaire design, pilot tests, training and publicity.
Coverage errors are omissions or duplications; content errors are wrong characteristics.
A post-enumeration survey estimates coverage and content error; net coverage rate = census count ÷ PES estimate × 100.
Census totals supply planning denominators and small-area data, but need projections between censuses.

en.title: Vital Registration and Vital Statistics
en.short: Civil registration of births, deaths and marriages, data quality, completeness and indirect estimation.

sections.heading: What the system is
sections.text: Civil registration is the continuous, permanent and compulsory recording of vital events by government, usually through local registrars. The main events are live births, deaths, marriages and stillbirths; some countries also record divorces and adoptions. Each record creates a legal document and a statistical record. Vital statistics are the counts, rates and characteristics compiled from those records, such as births by age of mother or deaths by cause. The legal rules differ by country, so check the national registration law and statistics office.

sections.heading: Completeness and quality
sections.text: Completeness is the share of actual events that are registered. It is often estimated as registered events ÷ estimated events × 100. If 4,500 births are registered and the estimated total is 5,000, completeness is 4,500 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 90%. Quality problems include late registration, missing dates or ages, duplicate records, and deaths with no certified cause. Cause-of-death data need a medical certificate and coding, usually with the International Classification of Diseases (ICD). Ill-defined causes and verbal autopsy, where a trained interviewer asks relatives about symptoms, are common where medical certification is limited.

sections.heading: When registration is incomplete
sections.text: Where registration is incomplete, demographers use indirect estimation from censuses and surveys. Examples include questions on children ever born and children surviving (summary birth histories), household deaths in a recent period, and orphanhood or widowhood questions. These methods estimate levels and patterns, not individual legal records. They depend on assumptions, so results are approximate. Completeness also varies by event and by region. Marriage registration also varies: religious and customary marriages may not be recorded, so survey data may be needed. Always state the country and year and check official sources.

keyPoints: Civil registration is the continuous, permanent and compulsory legal recording of vital events by government.
Vital statistics are the counts, rates and characteristics compiled from registration records.
Completeness = registered events ÷ estimated events × 100; if 4,500 of 5,000 births are registered, completeness is 90%.
Quality problems include underregistration, late registration, missing dates or ages, duplicate records and ill-defined causes of death.
Cause-of-death statistics need medical certification and ICD coding; verbal autopsy is used where certification is limited.
Indirect estimation from censuses and surveys can estimate birth and death levels when registration is incomplete, but results are approximate and country-specific.

en.title: Sample Surveys in Demography
en.short: This summary covers survey design, sampling frames, questionnaires, fieldwork, error, weighting and DHS/MICS estimates.

sections.heading: Frames and samples
sections.text:
A sampling frame is the list or map of population units from which a sample is drawn. It must be complete, current and free of duplicates; gaps cause coverage error. In probability sampling every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection, so results can be generalised and sampling error can be estimated.

Common designs are simple random, systematic, stratified and cluster or multistage sampling. Demographic surveys often use multistage cluster samples: first villages or Enumeration Areas, then households, then eligible people, because no full list of individuals exists.

sections.heading: Questionnaires and fieldwork
sections.text:
A questionnaire is a standardised set of questions. Good questionnaires are clear, pretested, translated carefully and use skip patterns so respondents answer only relevant questions.

Fieldwork needs trained interviewers, close supervision, back-checks and checks for missing or inconsistent answers. Non-sampling error covers coverage, non-response, measurement and processing errors. It can bias estimates, and a larger sample does not remove it.

sections.heading: Weighting and example
sections.text:
Weights adjust for unequal selection chances and non-response. A weight is roughly the inverse of a unit’s selection probability. A weighted mean is Σwx ÷ Σw.

Suppose 120 urban households have mean size 4.0 and weight 2, and 80 rural households have mean 6.0 and weight 5. Weighted mean = (120×2×4 + 80×5×6) ÷ (120×2 + 80×5) = 3360 ÷ 640 = 5.25. The unweighted mean is (120×4 + 80×6) ÷ 200 = 4.8. Weighting changes the estimate and usually raises its variance.

sections.heading: Programmes and estimates
sections.text:
Major international programmes include the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and UNICEF’s Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS); the World Bank runs the Living Standards Measurement Study (LSMS). National statistical offices run national household surveys.

A survey estimate is a sample statistic used to infer a population value. Report it with a confidence interval and the design, because clustering raises standard errors. Definitions and methods differ between surveys, so compare countries and years only after checking the official report.

keyPoints: A sampling frame must cover the target population without gaps or duplicates.
Probability sampling gives every unit a known non-zero chance, allowing sampling error to be estimated.
Non-sampling error includes coverage, non-response, measurement and processing errors and is not removed by a larger sample.
A weight is roughly the inverse selection probability; weighted mean = Σwx ÷ Σw.
DHS, MICS and LSMS are major survey programmes; national statistical offices run national surveys.
Survey estimates should be reported with confidence intervals and design details, and compared across surveys only after checking definitions.

en.title: Population Composition and Structure
en.short: Age and sex structure, population pyramids, dependency ratios, median age and sex ratios.

sections.heading: Age and sex structure
sections.text: Age structure is the distribution of a population by age group. Sex structure is its distribution by sex. Together they form the age-sex composition. A population pyramid is a graph with age groups on the vertical axis and males and females on opposite sides. Median age is the age that divides the population into two equal halves: half are younger and half are older. It is not the average age. The sex ratio is the number of males per 100 females: males ÷ females × 100. Age and sex structure reflect past fertility, mortality and migration, so it records a population’s history.

sections.heading: Reading pyramids
sections.text: A broad base and narrow top show an expansive pyramid, typical of high fertility and young population. A narrow base shows a constrictive pyramid, often after fertility has fallen. A roughly straight-sided pyramid is stationary. Compare the two sides: a bulge or dent may reflect migration, war or a baby boom. Describe the shape with percentages, not only counts, because total size varies. Age reporting can be inaccurate, especially where ages are heaped on round numbers.

sections.heading: Dependency and example
sections.text: The dependency ratio compares people usually outside the labour force with the working-age population. Using the common cut-offs, total dependency ratio = (ages 0-14 + ages 65 and over) ÷ ages 15-64 × 100. Child dependency uses only 0-14; old-age dependency uses only 65 and over. In a country with 420,000 children, 540,000 working-age people and 40,000 older people, child dependency = 420,000 ÷ 540,000 × 100 = 77.8. Old-age dependency = 40,000 ÷ 540,000 × 100 = 7.4. Total = 460,000 ÷ 540,000 × 100 = 85.2. If males are 490,000 and females 510,000, sex ratio = 490,000 ÷ 510,000 × 100 = 96.1. Interpret ratios with the age cut-offs and labour-force reality in mind; they are not direct measures of economic burden.

keyPoints: Age structure is the distribution by age group; sex structure is the distribution by sex.
A population pyramid plots age groups against males and females.
Median age divides the population into two equal halves by age, not the mean age.
Sex ratio = males ÷ females × 100.
Total dependency ratio = (0-14 + 65 and over) ÷ 15-64 × 100.
Interpret composition with percentages and note that age cut-offs and age reporting vary by country and data source.

en.title: Population Growth and Components of Change
en.short: Growth rates, exponential growth, doubling time and the balancing equation for natural increase and net migration.

sections.heading: Growth rates
sections.text:
A population growth rate measures how fast a population changes. For a single year, r = (P1 − P0) ÷ P0, where P0 is the starting population and P1 is the population one year later. Multiply by 100 for a percentage. A positive r means growth; a negative r means decline.

Exponential growth means a constant rate applied repeatedly, so the population compounds. In discrete years, Pt = P0(1 + r)^t. In continuous form, Pt = P0e^(rt), where e is about 2.718. Doubling time is the time needed to double at a constant rate. Exactly, for continuous growth, td = ln(2) ÷ r. The rule of 70 approximates it: td ≈ 70 ÷ (100r), with r as a decimal.

sections.heading: Components of change
sections.text:
The balancing equation separates the sources of change:
P1 = P0 + B − D + I − E.
B is births, D is deaths, I is immigration (people entering) and E is emigration (people leaving). Natural increase is B − D. Net migration is I − E. Total change is natural increase plus net migration. If net migration is negative, more people leave than enter, so it lowers the total change. This equation is an identity when the data are complete and the population is closed to unrecorded movement.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Suppose a country starts the year with 1,000,000 people. During the year there are 30,000 births, 12,000 deaths, 5,000 immigrants and 3,000 emigrants.
Natural increase = 30,000 − 12,000 = 18,000.
Net migration = 5,000 − 3,000 = 2,000.
Total change = 18,000 + 2,000 = 20,000.
End population = 1,000,000 + 20,000 = 1,020,000.
Growth rate = 20,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.02 = 2% per year.
Using continuous growth, r = ln(1.02) ≈ 0.0198. Doubling time ≈ ln(2) ÷ 0.0198 ≈ 35 years. The rule of 70 gives 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years.

keyPoints: Growth rate over one year is r = (P1 − P0) ÷ P0; multiply by 100 for a percentage.
Exponential growth is Pt = P0(1 + r)^t in discrete time or Pt = P0e^(rt) in continuous time.
Doubling time is approximately 70 ÷ (100r) years when r is a decimal, or exactly ln(2) ÷ r for continuous growth.
The balancing equation is P1 = P0 + B − D + I − E.
Natural increase is births minus deaths; net migration is immigration minus emigration.
Total population change equals natural increase plus net migration.

en.title: Fertility: Measurement and Determinants
en.short: Measuring fertility with CBR, ASFR, TFR and parity, plus biological, social, economic and proximate determinants.

sections.heading: Rates and ratios
sections.text: Fertility means actual births, not the biological capacity to bear children (fecundity). The crude birth rate (CBR) is B ÷ P × 1000, where B is births in a year and P is midyear population. It is easy to compute but mixes women of childbearing age with everyone else. The age-specific fertility rate (ASFR) is Bx ÷ Wx × 1000: births to women aged x divided by women aged x. It shows the age pattern of childbearing.

sections.heading: Total fertility
sections.text: The total fertility rate (TFR) is the sum of ASFRs over all ages, divided by 1000 when rates are per 1000. With five-year age groups, multiply the sum by 5 first. It is a synthetic cohort measure: the children a woman would have if current age-specific rates stayed fixed through her reproductive life. Example: ASFRs for ages 15-19 to 45-49 are 40, 120, 150, 110, 60, 20 and 5 per 1000. Sum = 505. TFR = 5 × 505 ÷ 1000 = 2.53 children per woman. TFR is not a prediction for any real woman.

sections.heading: Parity measures
sections.text: Parity is the number of children a woman has borne. The parity progression ratio (PPR) is the proportion of women of parity n who later have another birth. Mean parity is children ever born divided by women. The child-woman ratio uses children under five divided by women aged 15-49, often ×1000; it is affected by child mortality. These measures describe past fertility and are useful where birth registration is incomplete.

sections.heading: Determinants and differences
sections.text: Biological determinants include fecundity, age, gestation and postpartum infecundity, especially lactational amenorrhoea, the absence of periods while breastfeeding. Social determinants include marriage patterns, education and norms. Economic determinants include income, the cost of children, women’s employment and urban living. Bongaarts groups the main proximate determinants, the direct factors through which all other influences work, as exposure to intercourse, contraception, abortion and postpartum infecundability. Fertility usually differs by education, residence and wealth, but the direction varies by setting.

keyPoints: CBR = B ÷ P × 1000; it is affected by the whole population’s age structure.
ASFR = Bx ÷ Wx × 1000 measures fertility at each age.
TFR = Σ ASFR ÷ 1000 for single-year rates, or 5 × Σ ASFR ÷ 1000 for five-year groups.
A parity progression ratio is the share of women of parity n who have another birth.
Bongaarts’s proximate determinants are exposure to intercourse, contraception, induced abortion and postpartum infecundability.
Fertility differentials by education, residence and wealth vary across settings, so check local data.

en.title: Mortality: Measurement and Differentials
en.short: Measuring mortality: crude death rate, infant and under-five mortality, life expectancy, causes and data quality.

sections.heading: Core measures
sections.text: The crude death rate (CDR) is deaths in a year divided by the mid-year population, multiplied by 1,000. It is simple but strongly affected by age structure, so it is a poor comparison between a young and an old population. The infant mortality rate (IMR) is deaths before age one in a year divided by live births in that year, times 1,000. The under-five mortality rate (U5MR) uses deaths before age five and the same denominator. Both are expressed per 1,000 live births. Life expectancy at birth is the average years a newborn would live if current age-specific death rates stayed constant. It is a summary, not a forecast.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Suppose a country has a mid-year population of 1,000,000, 12,000 deaths, 40,000 live births, 2,400 infant deaths and 3,200 deaths under age five.
CDR = 12,000 ÷ 1,000,000 × 1,000 = 12 per 1,000.
IMR = 2,400 ÷ 40,000 × 1,000 = 60 per 1,000 live births.
U5MR = 3,200 ÷ 40,000 × 1,000 = 80 per 1,000 live births.
The infant deaths are included in the under-five deaths. Life expectancy cannot be calculated from these totals alone; it needs age-specific death rates.

sections.heading: Causes and differentials
sections.text: In low-income settings, communicable diseases, maternal and perinatal conditions and malnutrition cause many deaths. In higher-income settings, noncommunicable diseases and injuries dominate. Mortality differs by age, sex, education, income, place of residence and ethnicity. Women usually live longer than men, but maternal deaths raise mortality among young women. Children of mothers with more education and households with safe water generally face lower mortality.

sections.heading: Data and interpretation
sections.text: Death registration is often incomplete, especially for infants and rural deaths. Surveys such as the Demographic and Health Surveys, verbal autopsy (interviews with relatives about symptoms) and sibling histories help fill gaps, but recall error and misreporting remain. UN agencies adjust estimates. Interpret CDR with age structure in mind; compare IMR and U5MR because definitions and reporting differ. A falling IMR shows better child survival, but it does not prove that health services caused the change.

keyPoints: CDR = deaths in a year ÷ mid-year population × 1,000.
IMR = infant deaths in a year ÷ live births in the same year × 1,000.
U5MR = deaths under age five in a year ÷ live births in the same year × 1,000.
Life expectancy at birth is the average years lived under current age-specific death rates; it is not a forecast.
CDR is distorted by age structure, so compare age-specific or age-standardised rates.
Infant and under-five mortality are sensitive to data quality, so use adjusted survey and registration estimates with care.

en.title: Life Tables
en.short: Period and cohort life tables: columns, survival probabilities, life expectancy and uses.

sections.heading: Period and cohort tables
sections.text: A life table follows a group through age, showing deaths and survival. A period life table uses age-specific death rates observed in one calendar year and applies them to a hypothetical cohort. It describes mortality at that time, not the actual fate of a real group. A cohort life table follows a real group born in the same year, so it is complete only when all members have died. Period tables are common because they need data from one period; cohort tables are rarer and slower to complete. They compare mortality and feed projections.

sections.heading: Columns and construction
sections.text: Columns are: x, exact age; nqx, probability of dying between x and x+n; npx = 1 − nqx, probability of surviving; lx, survivors at exact age x from a radix such as 100,000; ndx = lx − lx+n, deaths in the interval; nLx, person-years lived in the interval; Tx, person-years remaining above x; and ex = Tx ÷ lx, life expectancy. To build a table, convert observed age-specific death rates nmx into nqx with nqx = n nmx ÷ [1 + n nmx(n − nax)], where nax is average years lived in the interval by those who die. Then set lx+n = lx(1 − nqx). Survival from birth to age x is lx ÷ l0.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Take a simplified one-year table with l0 = 1000, l1 = 800, l2 = 500 and l3 = 0. Then q0 = 200 ÷ 1000 = 0.200 and p0 = 0.800; q1 = 300 ÷ 800 = 0.375 and p1 = 0.625; q2 = 500 ÷ 500 = 1.000. Using Lx = (lx + lx+1) ÷ 2 gives L0 = 900, L1 = 650 and L2 = 250. T0 = 900 + 650 + 250 = 1800, so e0 = 1800 ÷ 1000 = 1.8 years. Also e1 = 900 ÷ 800 = 1.125 and e2 = 250 ÷ 500 = 0.5. So e0 = 1.8 years if these rates continued.

keyPoints: A period life table applies one period’s age-specific death rates to a hypothetical cohort; a cohort table follows a real group through life.
qx is the probability of dying in an age interval, px = 1 − qx is the probability of surviving it, and lx is the number surviving to exact age x from the radix.
Deaths in an interval are dx = lx − lx+n, person-years are Lx, and life expectancy is ex = Tx ÷ lx.
A common conversion is qx = mx ÷ (1 + 0.5mx) for one-year intervals under a mid-year assumption; more generally nqx = n nmx ÷ [1 + n nmx(n − nax)].
Survival from birth to age x is lx ÷ l0, and e0 is the average years a newborn would live if current mortality rates continued.
Life tables compare mortality, study survival, support population projections and are used in insurance and health analysis.

en.title: Migration and Mobility
en.short: Definitions, measures, data sources, determinants, selectivity and consequences of migration.

sections.heading: Types of migration
sections.text: Migration is a change of usual residence across a boundary, such as between districts or across a border. Internal migration is a move within one country, for example from a village to a city. International migration crosses a national border. An emigrant leaves a country; an immigrant enters one. Related mobility includes residential moves, circulation (temporary and repeated movement) and commuting, which is daily travel and not migration. Forced migration covers refugees and displaced people. Migrant stock is the number living outside their country of birth at a date; migration flow is the number of moves in a period.

sections.heading: Measuring migration
sections.text: For an area, in-migration (I) and out-migration (O) give net migration NM = I − O. Gross migration is G = I + O. The net migration rate is NM ÷ P × 1000, where P is the mid-year population. Example: P = 200,000, I = 8,000, O = 5,000. NM = 3,000. Net migration rate = 3,000 ÷ 200,000 × 1000 = 15 per 1000. In-migration rate = 40 per 1000; out-migration rate = 25 per 1000; gross rate = 65 per 1000. Data come from censuses (birthplace, previous residence), sample surveys, population registers in some countries, and border records. Each source has coverage problems, especially for undocumented moves.

sections.heading: Determinants and selectivity
sections.text: Push factors drive people out: low wages, unemployment, conflict, disaster. Pull factors attract: jobs, safety, services, family. Intervening obstacles such as cost, borders and language shape who actually moves. Migration is selective: young adults, the better educated and those with networks are often over-represented, and sex selectivity varies by stream. A nurse moving from Ghana to the United Kingdom illustrates skill selectivity.

sections.heading: Consequences
sections.text: Sending areas may gain remittances (money migrants send home) and ideas but lose skilled workers (brain drain) and face changed households. Receiving areas gain labour and diversity but may face housing pressure and integration tasks. Effects depend on scale, skills and policy.

keyPoints: Migration is a change of usual residence; internal moves stay within a country, international moves cross a border.
Net migration = in-migration − out-migration; gross migration = in-migration + out-migration.
Net migration rate = net migration ÷ mid-year population × 1000.
Censuses, surveys, population registers and border records measure migration, each with coverage limits.
Push and pull factors, obstacles and networks shape migration, and migrants are selective by age, skill and sex.
Sending areas may gain remittances but lose skills; receiving areas gain labour but face integration costs.

en.title: Nuptiality, Family and Households
en.short: Marriage, union formation, divorce, household structure and their demographic links.

sections.heading: Nuptiality and family terms
sections.text: Nuptiality is the study of marriage and union formation: when people start unions, what type, and how they end. A family is usually a group related by blood, marriage or adoption, though definitions vary by country and survey; a household is people who share a dwelling and housekeeping. The two overlap but are not the same. Key measures include the proportion ever married, the proportion currently married, age at first marriage, and the singulate mean age at marriage (SMAM), the average years lived single before first marriage in a synthetic cohort (a made-up group followed at current rates).

sections.heading: Measuring marriage
sections.text: Age at marriage is often measured from census or survey data on marital status by age. The proportion married at each age shows the timing of union formation. SMAM uses the proportion never married at exact ages 15, 20, 25 and so on up to 50. With grouped data, SMAM = 15 + [5 × sum of the proportions never married − 0.5 S50] ÷ (1 − S50), where S50 is the proportion never married at 50. If nobody is still single at 50, this reduces to 15 plus 5 times the sum.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Example: proportions never married at ages 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45 and 50 are 0.80, 0.40, 0.10, 0.02, 0, 0, 0 and 0. Sum = 1.32. Multiply by 5 = 6.60. No one remains single at 50, so SMAM = 15 + 6.60 = 21.6 years. A higher SMAM means later marriage. Check: 0.80 + 0.40 + 0.10 + 0.02 = 1.32; 1.32 × 5 = 6.60; 15 + 6.60 = 21.60.

sections.heading: Households and change
sections.text: Divorce, separation and widowhood end unions and change household structure. Households may be nuclear, extended, single-person or headed by a woman or man. Family change includes later marriage, more cohabitation in some countries, and more divorce, but patterns differ by country and income. Household structure affects demographic behaviour: early marriage can lengthen exposure to childbearing; female-headed households may face different health and poverty risks; older people living alone may need different care. Always check current national survey definitions.

keyPoints: Nuptiality is the study of marriage and union formation, including timing, type and dissolution.
A family is based on kinship; a household is based on shared dwelling and housekeeping.
Proportion ever married = ever married people ÷ all people in the age group.
SMAM = 15 + [5 × sum of five-year proportions never married − 0.5 S50] ÷ (1 − S50), where S50 is the proportion never married at 50.
Later marriage usually shortens exposure to childbearing, but other factors also matter.
Household structure and demographic behaviour influence each other, and patterns vary by country.

en.title: Population Estimates and Projections
en.short: Inter-censal estimates, cohort-component projections, assumptions, scenarios, error and planning uses.

sections.heading: Inter-censal estimates
sections.text: An inter-censal estimate gives population between two censuses. The simplest method uses the balancing equation or a constant growth rate. The balancing equation is P(t) = P(0) + births - deaths + net migration. If census counts are P(0) at time 0 and P(t) at time t, then r = ln[P(t) ÷ P(0)] ÷ t and P(s) = P(0) × e^(r × s). For example, 10.0 million in 2010 and 12.0 million in 2020 give r = ln(1.2) ÷ 10 = 0.01823. The 2015 estimate is 10.0 × e^(0.01823 × 5) = 10.95 million. This assumes smooth constant growth.

sections.heading: Cohort-component method
sections.text: The cohort-component method projects each age and sex group forward. Survivors are carried to the next age using life-table survival ratios: P(t+1, a+1) = P(t, a) × S(a) + net migrants of the same ages. Births come from age-specific fertility rates applied to women of childbearing age: B = Σ ASFR(a) × W(a). The births are survived to age 0 in the next period. The method needs a base population, a life table, fertility rates and migration assumptions.

sections.heading: Assumptions and scenarios
sections.text: Projections are conditional on assumptions, not forecasts. Fertility assumptions may follow a total fertility rate path, mortality assumptions a life expectancy path, and migration a net number or rate. Scenario building varies these inputs to show a range: low, medium and high fertility, faster or slower mortality decline, or more or less migration. A policy scenario can test what happens if family planning or health services expand. Each scenario must state its assumptions clearly.

sections.heading: Error and planning
sections.text: Projection error grows with the horizon. Fertility is usually the largest source of uncertainty, migration is volatile, and census undercount or age misreporting affects the base. Errors in assumptions compound. Projections are used in planning schools, health services, housing, pensions, labour supply and elections. Planners should use a range, check against new data, and revise. A projection is a tool for asking what if, not a promise about the future.

keyPoints: Inter-censal estimates use the balancing equation or a constant growth rate; for constant growth, r = ln[P(t) ÷ P(0)] ÷ t and P(s) = P(0) × e^(r × s).
The cohort-component method survives each age-sex group and adds births and net migration.
Births are projected as B = Σ ASFR(a) × W(a), then survived to age 0.
Fertility, mortality and migration assumptions drive every projection, so scenarios show a range rather than one certain future.
Projection error grows with time and is largest when fertility and migration are uncertain.
Projections guide planning for schools, health, housing, pensions and labour, but they must be revised as data improve.

en.title: Demographic Transition and Population Theory
en.short: Classic transition model, variants, criticisms, and theories of fertility, mortality and migration.

sections.heading: Classic model
sections.text: The classic demographic transition model describes a shift from high birth and death rates to low ones. It has four stages. In stage 1, birth and death rates are high, so natural increase (births minus deaths) is near zero. In stage 2, death rates fall while birth rates stay high, so population grows fast. In stage 3, birth rates fall and growth slows. In stage 4, both rates are low and population is nearly stationary. Some versions add a fifth stage of below-replacement fertility and ageing. It describes European experience, not a law.

sections.heading: Variants and criticisms
sections.text: Variants include the five-stage version and the second demographic transition, which links low fertility to changing values, gender roles and family forms. The epidemiological transition describes changing causes of death, from infectious to chronic disease. Critics say the model is Eurocentric, assumes one path, and ignores migration, policy, war, culture and inequality. Countries may stall or reverse. It predicts direction, not timing.

sections.heading: Population theories
sections.text: Population theory debates the relation between population and resources. Thomas Malthus argued that population tends to grow faster than food, checked by famine, disease and restraint. Ester Boserup reversed the link: population pressure can induce agricultural innovation. Neo-Malthusians stress environmental limits; critics stress technology, institutions and consumption. Demographic transition theory is a population theory: fertility falls with development, but ideas, gender and policy also matter.

sections.heading: Fertility, mortality, migration
sections.text: Fertility debates contrast demand for children with supply of contraception and diffusion of new norms. Mortality debates ask whether medicine or living standards drove decline; McKeown emphasised nutrition, while others stress public health and vaccines. Migration theories include push-pull, neoclassical wage gaps, new economics of labour migration and world-systems accounts. Example: if the death rate falls from 25 to 12 per 1,000 while the birth rate stays at 40, natural increase rises from 15 to 28 per 1,000. Check: 40 − 25 = 15; 40 − 12 = 28.

keyPoints: The classic transition has four stages from high to low birth and death rates; some versions add a fifth.
Natural increase equals birth rate minus death rate; stage 2 growth is fastest because deaths fall before births.
The model describes European experience and predicts direction, not timing; it is not a universal law.
Variants include the five-stage model, second demographic transition and epidemiological transition.
Malthus argued population outruns food; Boserup argued population pressure can induce innovation.
Fertility, mortality and migration debates involve demand, diffusion, medicine, living standards, push-pull and political economy.

en.title: Population and Development: Growth, Structure and Debate
en.short: Debates on population growth, age structure, poverty and environment.

sections.heading: Growth and development
sections.text: Development means lasting gains in income, health, education and choice, not income alone. Population growth can raise the labour force and demand, but it also raises the need for schools, clinics, jobs and food. Whether it helps depends on institutions, technology, the age structure and the environment. It also changes the dependency burden. A larger population is not automatically a problem or a benefit.

sections.heading: Malthus and Boserup
sections.text: Thomas Malthus (1798) argued that population tends to outrun food supply, so famine, disease and restraint keep numbers in check. Ester Boserup (1965) reversed the emphasis: population pressure can push farmers to intensify land use and innovate. Evidence is mixed. Some densely settled areas have raised yields; others have suffered soil exhaustion and falling yields. Neither theory fits every place.

sections.heading: Demographic dividend
sections.text: A demographic dividend is the economic gain that can follow a fall in birth rates. The age structure shifts, so there are more working-age people relative to children and older dependants. This can raise saving and output per person. But the dividend is not automatic: it needs jobs, education, health care and stable government. Without these, a youth-heavy population may bring unemployment instead.

sections.heading: Poverty and environment
sections.text: Rapid growth does not by itself cause or cure poverty. Poverty depends heavily on distribution, employment, education and social protection. Environmental impact is often summarised as I = P × A × T: impact equals population × affluence × technology. Population is one multiplier, not the only cause. Suppose Amina’s rural district grows: more fuelwood demand can damage woodland, but better stoves and tree planting can reduce it. Policy, not population size alone, shapes the outcome.

keyPoints: Malthus argued population tends to outrun food supply; Boserup argued population pressure can drive agricultural intensification.
Evidence on both theories is mixed and context-dependent.
A demographic dividend arises when a falling birth rate lowers the dependency burden and raises the share of working-age people.
The dividend is not automatic; it requires jobs, education, health care and good governance.
Poverty and environmental damage depend on distribution, technology and policy, not population size alone.
IPAT summarises environmental impact as I = P × A × T.

en.title: Population Policy and Programmes
en.short: Rationale, types, design, delivery, evaluation and ethics of population policies and programmes.

sections.heading: Why have a policy
sections.text:
A population policy is a deliberate set of government measures that affect population size, growth, composition or distribution. A programme is the organised services and activities that carry the policy out.

The rationale is to align demographic change with development goals such as health, education, jobs, housing and the environment. Policies may target births, deaths, migration, ageing or where people live, so not every population policy is about fertility.

sections.heading: Types and tools
sections.text:
Types include pro-natalist policies, which aim to raise births; anti-natalist policies, which aim to slow growth; family planning and reproductive health policies; migration and settlement policies; ageing policies; and policies to change population distribution. Instruments include information and education, services, incentives such as cash or tax relief, legal rules on marriage, abortion or immigration, and coercion. Coercion is rare and ethically grave.

Aims vary: China used a one-child policy from about 1980 to 2015; France uses family benefits to support births; many African countries place family planning within development plans.

sections.heading: Design and delivery
sections.text:
Design starts with the problem and target group, then sets measurable objectives, chooses instruments, estimates cost, checks legal authority and plans monitoring. Delivery involves ministries, local government, clinics, schools, NGOs and community leaders.

Suppose Amina, a district officer in a fictional country called Bara, and Chidi, a clinic nurse, run a programme to raise contraceptive use among young married couples. They first survey use and unmet need, train nurses, send radio messages in local languages, offer vouchers and track stock-outs monthly.

sections.heading: Evaluation and ethics
sections.text:
Evaluation compares outcomes with a baseline or comparison group. Indicators may include contraceptive prevalence, unmet need, births, migration and service quality. Good evaluation also checks cost, coverage and unintended effects.

Ethics require voluntary choice, informed consent, confidentiality, equity and protection from stigma. Coercive targets, such as sterilisation quotas, are widely condemned. Policy aims and instruments differ by country because history, religion, economy and politics differ, so students should check the current official policy rather than assume one model.

keyPoints: A population policy is a deliberate set of government measures affecting population size, growth, composition or distribution.
Instruments range from information and services to incentives and legal rules, and coercive measures raise serious ethical problems.
Design needs a clear target group, measurable objectives, budget, legal authority and a monitoring plan.
Implementation depends on ministries, local services, NGOs and community trust, not only on a law.
Evaluation compares outcomes with a baseline or comparison group and checks unintended effects.
Policy aims vary by country: China used a one-child policy from about 1980 to 2015, while France uses family benefits to support births.

en.title: Family Planning, Unmet Need and Reproductive Health
en.short: Family planning concepts, unmet need, service delivery, reproductive rights and programme evaluation.

sections.heading: Family planning and unmet need
sections.text:
Family planning is the deliberate effort by individuals or couples to decide whether and when to have children, and how many. Methods include modern contraception, fertility awareness and treatment of infertility; the choice belongs to the user. A key indicator is unmet need: women who are sexually active, want to avoid or delay pregnancy, and are not using any method. Surveys such as the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) estimate it, but definitions and denominators vary, so compare like with like.

Suppose a hypothetical district surveys 5,000 married or in-union women. Of these, 1,800 use a modern method and 1,200 want to avoid or delay pregnancy but use no method. Unmet need = 1,200 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 24%. Modern contraceptive prevalence (mCPR) = 1,800 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 36%. Demand satisfied = 1,800 ÷ (1,800 + 1,200) × 100 = 60%.

sections.heading: Reproductive health and rights
sections.text: Reproductive health is a state of physical, mental and social wellbeing in matters of reproduction, not merely the absence of disease. The 1994 International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD) in Cairo set out reproductive rights: people should decide freely and responsibly on the number and spacing of children and have access to the information and services to do so, without coercion or discrimination. This makes reproductive health both a public health issue and a rights issue. Rights language does not require any particular method; it requires informed choice, privacy, consent and safety.

sections.heading: Services and evaluation
sections.text: Service delivery can be public, private or non-governmental, and may be clinic-based, community-based or integrated with other health services. Good delivery covers supply chains, trained staff, counselling, confidentiality and reach to young people, rural and poor groups. Programme evaluation asks whether services were implemented as planned (process), whether use and unmet need changed (outcome), and whether health and wellbeing improved (impact). A credible comparison group or counterfactual strengthens causal claims; before-and-after figures alone can mislead.

keyPoints: Unmet need is the share of women who want to avoid or delay pregnancy but use no method.
Contraceptive prevalence rate = current users ÷ women in the denominator × 100.
Demand satisfied = users ÷ (users + unmet need) × 100, using consistent definitions.
Reproductive health is a public health and rights issue, not merely birth control.
Service delivery needs supply, counselling, privacy and reach to underserved groups.
Evaluation looks at process, outcomes and impact; causal claims need a credible counterfactual.

en.title: Health Demography and Epidemiology
en.short: Morbidity, disability, health expectancy, the epidemiological transition and health data for population health.

sections.heading: Morbidity and disability
sections.text: Health demography studies how health states are distributed in populations. Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of disease, injury and death. Morbidity means illness or disease in a population, not only death. Disability means a limitation in activity or functioning, such as difficulty walking or working; it is not the same as a diagnosis. Prevalence is existing cases at a time divided by the population. Incidence is new cases over a period divided by the population at risk, often per 1,000 person-years.

sections.heading: Health expectancy
sections.text: Health expectancy estimates how many years a person can expect to live in good health. Healthy life expectancy and disability-free life expectancy are common forms. The Sullivan method combines age-specific prevalence of poor health with life-table survival. In a simplified illustration, suppose 200 of 1,000 people report a disability, so prevalence is 200 ÷ 1,000 = 0.20, or 20%. If life expectancy at birth is 60 years, disability-free life expectancy is about 60 × (1 − 0.20) = 48 years, leaving 12 years with disability.

sections.heading: Epidemiological transition
sections.text: The epidemiological transition is Omran’s theory that populations move from high death rates dominated by infectious disease and famine to lower death rates dominated by chronic and degenerative diseases. Omran described ages of pestilence and famine, receding pandemics, and degenerative and man-made diseases. Later writers add delayed degenerative stages. Timing and pattern vary by country and are not one universal path. The theory helps explain why cause-of-death patterns change as mortality falls.

sections.heading: Using health data
sections.text: Health data are used to compare population health and mortality patterns. Surveys measure self-reported illness, disability and risk factors. Vital registration and surveillance record deaths and cases. Cause-specific mortality rates show which diseases kill most in each age and sex group. Case fatality compares deaths with diagnosed cases. For example, 50 new cases among 5,000 people at risk in one year give an incidence rate of 50 ÷ 5,000 = 0.01, or 10 per 1,000 person-years. Data quality matters.

keyPoints: Morbidity is illness or disease in a population; disability is a limitation in activity or functioning.
Prevalence = existing cases ÷ population at a time; incidence rate = new cases ÷ person-time at risk.
Health expectancy estimates years lived in good health by combining health prevalence with life-table survival, as in the Sullivan method.
Omran’s epidemiological transition describes a long-term shift from infectious to chronic causes of death, but timing varies by country.
Health surveys, vital registration and surveillance are used to compare cause-specific mortality and population health patterns.
In the simplified example, 200 disabled among 1,000 gives 20% prevalence; with life expectancy 60, disability-free expectancy is about 48 years.

en.title: Urbanisation and Spatial Demography
en.short: Urban growth, rural-urban migration, spatial distribution, measures of urbanisation and planning implications.

sections.heading: Urban growth and migration
sections.text: Urbanisation is the rising share of a population living in urban areas. Urban growth is the absolute increase in the number of urban residents. The two can differ: a country may add urban people while its urban share stays flat if the rural population grows at the same rate. Rural-urban migration is movement from countryside to towns, driven by push factors such as limited land and pull factors such as jobs and services. Urban growth also comes from natural increase and from reclassification, when a settlement is redefined as urban. Spatial demography studies how population is spread across territory: density, concentration and the size and spacing of settlements.

sections.heading: Measuring urbanisation
sections.text:
Common measures are:
Percentage urban = (urban population ÷ total population) × 100.
Urban growth rate = ((U_t − U_0) ÷ U_0) × 100 over the period.
Rate of urbanisation = percentage urban at t − percentage urban at 0, usually in percentage points.
Suppose a country has 50 million people, 20 million urban: 40% urban. Ten years later it has 60 million people, 30 million urban: 50% urban. Urban growth = (30 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 50%. Total growth = (60 − 50) ÷ 50 × 100 = 20%. Rate of urbanisation = 50 − 40 = 10 percentage points over the decade, about 1 point a year. Rural population stayed at 30 million. Comparisons need care because countries define urban differently.

sections.heading: Distribution and planning
sections.text: Spatial distribution can be summarised by density, by the share of the population in the largest city (primacy), and by the rank-size pattern of towns (the rank-size rule: the nth largest settlement is roughly 1/n the size of the largest). Planning uses these measures to site housing, transport, water, sanitation, schools and clinics. Rapid urban growth can outpace infrastructure, producing overcrowding and informal settlements. Spatial planning also links towns and rural areas through roads, markets and service delivery. Countries vary widely. Some are mostly rural and some mostly urban; definitions, census dates and settlement patterns differ. Planning must therefore use current national data, not borrowed thresholds.

keyPoints: Urbanisation is the rising urban share; urban growth is the absolute increase in urban residents.
Urban growth comes from rural-urban migration, natural increase and reclassification.
Percentage urban = (urban population ÷ total population) × 100.
Rate of urbanisation is the change in percentage urban, usually in percentage points.
Spatial demography describes density, concentration, primacy and settlement patterns.
Planning must use national definitions and current data because urban definitions and levels vary by country.

en.title: Population Ageing
en.short: Individual and population ageing, old-age dependency, causes and consequences for families, labour, health and policy.

sections.heading: Individual and population
sections.text:
Individual ageing is the process of growing older over a life course. Chronological age is years since birth; biological and functional ageing refer to changes in health and capacity. Population ageing is a shift in the age structure towards older ages, shown by a rising median age and a rising share of people above an old-age threshold, commonly 65 though some countries use 60.

The two are linked but distinct. A population can age even if individual life spans do not change, because fewer births reduce the number of young people.

sections.heading: Measuring ageing
sections.text:
Common measures are the percentage aged 65 and over, the median age, and the old-age dependency ratio (OADR). The OADR is the number of people aged 65 and over per 100 people aged 15 to 64:
OADR = (P65+ ÷ P15-64) × 100.

Suppose a country has 8 million people aged 65 and over and 40 million aged 15 to 64. OADR = (8 ÷ 40) × 100 = 20 per 100. If the older group rises to 10 million while the working-age group stays at 40 million, OADR = (10 ÷ 40) × 100 = 25 per 100. The ratio is not a support ratio: not everyone aged 15 to 64 works, and some older people do.

sections.heading: Why populations age
sections.text: Fertility decline is the main cause. Fewer births shrink the young cohorts, so the older share rises. Falling mortality, especially at older ages, adds more survivors to old age. Migration can make a population younger or older, but its effect is usually smaller. This is part of the demographic transition.

sections.heading: Consequences and policy
sections.text: Families may face more care work, often by women. Labour markets may have fewer young workers and more older workers, so retirement ages and pensions matter. Health systems shift towards chronic disease and long-term care. Policy responses include pension reform, later retirement, support for carers, age-friendly environments and migration. Effects vary by country and resources.

keyPoints: Individual ageing is growing older over a life course; population ageing is a shift in the age structure towards older ages.
Fertility decline is the main cause of population ageing, with falling old-age mortality also contributing.
The old-age dependency ratio is (population aged 65+ ÷ population aged 15-64) × 100.
A rising OADR does not by itself show how many people actually work or need care.
Population ageing affects family care, labour supply, pensions and health systems.
Policy responses include pension reform, later retirement, carer support and age-friendly environments, and they vary by country.

en.title: Social Statistics and Social Indicators
en.short: Measuring social variables, building and reading indicators and composite indices, and judging data quality.

sections.heading: Variables and indicators
sections.text: A social variable is any characteristic measured for people, households or places, such as school completion, employment status or access to water. A social indicator is a single statistic chosen to show a condition and, usually, to track change. Indicators can be direct (the share of adults who can read) or indirect (books per child in a household). Official social statistics are figures produced by government agencies, often from censuses, surveys and administrative records. Their definitions and collection years differ by country, so always read the metadata, the notes that define the figure.

sections.heading: Composite indices
sections.text: A composite index combines several indicators into one number. The usual steps are: state the concept; select indicators; check direction; normalise each indicator to a common scale; choose weights; aggregate; and test sensitivity. Min-max normalisation for a higher-is-better indicator is (x − min) ÷ (max − min). Example: two districts score on school completion, immunisation and water access. A: 80, 70, 60. B: 60, 90, 80. Normalised A: 1, 0, 0. Normalised B: 0, 1, 1. With equal weights, A = (1 + 0 + 0) ÷ 3 = 0.333 and B = (0 + 1 + 1) ÷ 3 = 0.667, so B ranks higher. With weights 0.6, 0.2 and 0.2, A = 0.600 and B = 0.400, so A ranks higher. Weights are value judgements, not facts.

sections.heading: Quality and comparison
sections.text: Data quality has several dimensions: coverage (who is missing), accuracy, timeliness, comparability and coherence. A figure can be accurate for its own definition yet misleading in a comparison. Changes in survey questions, age limits or administrative rules can create breaks in a time series. Cross-country comparisons need harmonised definitions and, for money, a stated conversion basis. Report the source, year, definition and margin of uncertainty. Composite indices hide trade-offs, so show the component indicators beside the rank.

keyPoints: A social indicator is a single statistic used to describe or track a social condition; a composite index combines several indicators.
Min-max normalisation for a higher-is-better indicator is (x − min) ÷ (max − min).
A weighted composite is Σ(w_i × s_i) ÷ Σw_i, where s_i is the normalised score.
Weights and indicator choice are value judgements, so test sensitivity and report components.
Data quality depends on coverage, accuracy, timeliness, comparability and coherence, not just the headline number.
Compare places and years only after checking definitions, collection methods and metadata; official practices vary by country.

en.title: Demographic Data Analysis: Exploration and Multivariate Models
en.short: Cross-tabulation, regression and logistic regression for demographic data, with interpretation and quality checks.

sections.heading: Exploring data
sections.text: Start with exploratory analysis: check distributions, missing values, outliers and inconsistent categories before modelling. Cross-tabulation counts cases in two or more categorical variables. Report row or column percentages, not just counts, and state which. A chi-square test asks whether association exists, but it does not measure its strength. For a 2×2 table, the odds ratio summarises association: OR = (a×d) ÷ (b×c). Example: if 40 of 100 women and 20 of 100 men use a service, OR = (40×80) ÷ (60×20) = 3200 ÷ 1200 = 2.67. Women have 2.67 times the odds of use. This is association, not proof of cause.

sections.heading: Regression models
sections.text: Multiple linear regression models a continuous outcome, such as children ever born, as y = b0 + b1x1 + ... + bk xk + e. Each coefficient is the expected change in y for a one-unit rise in x, holding other variables fixed. Logistic regression models a binary outcome, such as whether a woman uses contraception. It estimates log odds: log(p ÷ (1−p)) = b0 + b1x1 + ... . Exponentiate a coefficient to get an odds ratio: exp(b). An OR above 1 means higher odds; below 1 means lower odds. Example: b = 0.693 gives exp(0.693) = 2.00, so one unit more x doubles the odds, other things equal. Do not say it doubles the probability. For complex surveys, use weights and design information if available.

sections.heading: Quality and reporting
sections.text: Check data quality before trusting results: coverage, non-response, missingness, recall error, age heaping (ages rounded to numbers ending in 0 or 5) and inconsistent reporting. State how missing data were handled. Avoid causal language for cross-sectional associations. Report sample size, model, reference categories, confidence intervals and whether weights were used. Present percentages to one decimal place at most and coefficients with units. A clear table and a short interpretation are better than many tests.

keyPoints: Cross-tabulation shows joint distributions; for a 2×2 table report the odds ratio (a×d) ÷ (b×c).
Linear regression: y = b0 + b1x1 + ... + bk xk + e; a coefficient is a change in the mean outcome holding other variables fixed.
Logistic regression: log(p ÷ (1−p)) = b0 + b1x1 + ...; exp(b) is an odds ratio, not a probability.
Check data quality, missingness and survey design before modelling.
Report sample size, reference groups, confidence intervals and weights, and avoid causal claims from cross-sectional associations.

en.title: Research Design, Ethics and the Project
en.short: Formulating demographic questions, reviewing literature, designing surveys, fieldwork ethics and reporting.

sections.heading: From idea to question
sections.text:
A demographic research question names the population, place, time and variables. Instead of “Does migration matter?”, ask: “Among adults aged 20 to 29 in a named town in 2025, is mobile money use associated with intention to migrate within five years?” Check that it is feasible, ethical and answerable with data. A literature review is a focused search and summary of earlier studies. It shows what is known, which methods were used and where a gap remains. Write a short conceptual framework linking your variables.

Case: Amina wants to study youth migration in a Nigerian town. She narrows her question, reads studies on migration intentions, and finds few local studies on mobile money.

sections.heading: Design and tools
sections.text: Choose a design that fits the question. A cross-sectional survey measures people at one time and suits prevalence and association. A cohort or longitudinal design follows the same people to study change. Define the target population and a sampling frame, the list from which you sample. Probability sampling lets you generalise; non-probability sampling does not. Sample size depends on the precision wanted, variability, design effect (the precision lost when clusters are sampled instead of individuals) and expected non-response. Draft the questionnaire, translate it carefully, pre-test it, and avoid leading or double-barrelled questions. Put sensitive items later and offer privacy.

sections.heading: Ethics in fieldwork
sections.text: Informed consent means telling participants the purpose, procedures, risks, benefits and how data will be used, then obtaining voluntary agreement. Consent must be documented; participants may withdraw without penalty. Confidentiality means protecting participants’ identities, for example by removing or coding names, storing data securely and limiting access. Seek ethics committee approval before fieldwork. Train interviewers, supervise them, check completed forms daily and back-check a sample by re-interviewing some respondents. Record refusals and missing data.

sections.heading: Writing the report
sections.text: The report should state the question, literature, design, sampling, questionnaire, fieldwork, ethics and limitations. Report response rates and missing data honestly. Discuss what the findings can and cannot support, then give references in the required style.

keyPoints: A good demographic question specifies population, place, time, variables and the relationship being studied.
A literature review identifies the gap and informs the design, not just summarises earlier work.
Cross-sectional surveys suit prevalence and association; cohort designs suit change over time.
Probability sampling supports generalisation, and sample size depends on precision, variability, design effect and non-response.
Informed consent must be voluntary, documented and revocable; confidentiality requires removing or coding identifying details and secure storage.
Report methods, response rates, ethics and limitations transparently.

en.title: Advanced Demographic Methods
en.short: Standardisation, decomposition, indirect estimation, smoothing, multistate models and data evaluation.
