sections.heading: Standardisation
sections.text:
Standardisation compares rates when age structures differ. Direct standardisation applies age-specific rates m_i to standard weights w_i: rate = Σ(m_i w_i) ÷ Σw_i. It needs reliable age-specific rates. Indirect standardisation uses standard rates to get expected deaths, then SMR = observed ÷ expected. It suits small or incomplete populations, but SMR is a ratio, not a rate, and depends on the standard.

Example: rates 0.01 and 0.10. A: 1000 young, 1000 old; crude = (10+100)÷2000 = 0.055. B: 2000 young, 1000 old; crude = (20+100)÷3000 = 0.04. Direct standardisation to 1000 young and 1000 old gives both 0.055: the gap was age structure.

sections.heading: Decomposition and smoothing
sections.text:
Decomposition splits a difference or change into components. The Kitagawa method separates a crude-rate difference into a rate component and an age-composition component. It is appropriate when asking whether mortality or ageing explains a gap. It is descriptive, not causal, and depends on the grouping used.

Smoothing removes random fluctuation from age-specific rates, using moving averages, splines or model life tables. It helps when rates are noisy, as in small areas. It can erase real irregularities, so the method should be reported.

sections.heading: Indirect estimation
sections.text: Indirect estimation derives measures from incomplete data. Examples include child survivorship to estimate child mortality, orphanhood to estimate adult mortality, and model life tables to convert one indicator into another. It suits incomplete vital registration. It is approximate: it relies on stable-population or model-table assumptions and accurate reporting.

sections.heading: Multistate and evaluation
sections.text:
Multistate methods model movement between states such as health, marital status or region. A multistate life table needs transition rates and usually a Markov assumption: the next state depends on the present state, not the full past. It suits disability and pension projections, but is data-hungry and sensitive to that assumption.

Evaluation checks data before use. Checks include age heaping (Whipple and Myers indices), sex ratios, cohort-component consistency and comparison with independent sources. Evaluation cannot create good data; it only shows where error is likely.

keyPoints: Direct standardisation: standardised rate = Σ(m_i w_i) ÷ Σw_i.
Indirect standardisation: SMR = observed deaths ÷ expected deaths, with expected = Σ(P_i M_i).
Kitagawa decomposition separates a crude-rate difference into rate and age-composition parts.
Indirect estimation is approximate and depends on stable-population or model life table assumptions.
Smoothing reduces random noise but can hide real age patterns.
Multistate models need transition rates and a Markov assumption; data evaluation checks age heaping, coverage and consistency.

en.title: Event History and Survival Analysis
en.short: Survival and hazard, censoring, Kaplan-Meier, Cox regression and demographic event applications.

sections.heading: Survival and hazard
sections.text: Event history analysis studies the time until an event, such as a birth, death or migration. T is the duration from a starting point to the event. The survival function S(t) = P(T > t) gives the chance of remaining event-free beyond t. The hazard h(t) is the immediate risk of the event at t, given survival to t: h(t) = lim Δt→0 P(t ≤ T < t + Δt | T ≥ t) ÷ Δt. The cumulative hazard is H(t) = −ln S(t).

sections.heading: Censoring and Kaplan-Meier
sections.text: Censoring occurs when the event is not observed before the study ends or the person leaves. Right censoring means we know only that T is greater than the recorded time. Kaplan-Meier estimates S(t) without assuming a shape. At each event time t_i, let d_i be the number of events and n_i the number at risk. Then S(t) = ∏(1 − d_i ÷ n_i) over event times up to t. Example: four people have times 2 (event), 4 (event), 4 (censored), 6 (censored). At t = 2: S = 1 − 1÷4 = 0.75. At t = 4: S = 0.75 × (1 − 1÷3) = 0.50. The median survival is 4.

sections.heading: Cox regression
sections.text: Cox regression models the hazard as h(t|X) = h0(t) exp(β1X1 + … + βkXk). h0(t) is an unspecified baseline hazard. The model assumes proportional hazards: the hazard ratio for two people is constant over time. exp(β) is a hazard ratio; a value above 1 means a higher hazard. Coefficients are estimated by partial likelihood, which avoids specifying h0(t). Check proportional hazards with Schoenfeld residuals or plots of log(−log S(t)).

sections.heading: Demographic applications
sections.text: These methods fit demographic event data. In fertility, the hazard of a next birth models birth intervals and parity progression. In mortality, survival after diagnosis or treatment is common. In migration, the hazard of moving models duration of stay. Event history handles time-varying covariates, such as age or employment, better than fixed-time models.

keyPoints: The survival function S(t) = P(T > t) gives the probability of no event by time t, and the hazard h(t) is the immediate event risk given survival to t.
Right censoring means the event time is known only to exceed the recorded time, and Kaplan-Meier assumes censoring is independent of the event process.
Kaplan-Meier: S(t) = ∏(1 − d_i ÷ n_i) over event times up to t, where d_i is events and n_i is the risk set.
Cox regression: h(t|X) = h0(t) exp(β1X1 + … + βkXk), with h0(t) unspecified and exp(β) the hazard ratio.
The proportional hazards assumption means hazard ratios stay constant over time; check it with Schoenfeld residuals or log(−log S(t)) plots.
Event history applies to fertility, mortality and migration by modelling durations to birth, death or movement, including time-varying covariates.

en.title: Causal Inference and Programme Evaluation
en.short: Covers counterfactual thinking, trials, difference-in-differences, IV and propensity scores for programme evaluation.

sections.heading: Counterfactual thinking
sections.text: Causal inference asks what would have happened without a programme. Each person has two potential outcomes: Y(1) with treatment and Y(0) without. The counterfactual is the outcome we do not observe. The average treatment effect is E[Y(1) − Y(0)]. Because we never see both outcomes for the same person, evaluation needs a credible comparison group. Selection bias occurs when treated and untreated people differ in ways that affect the outcome.

sections.heading: Randomised trials
sections.text: A randomised controlled trial assigns treatment by chance, so measured and unmeasured confounders balance in expectation. It estimates the intention-to-treat effect when analysed by assignment. Non-compliance, cost and ethics can limit trials. In population and health programmes, randomisation may be at clinic, village or district level. Cluster trials need enough clusters, and analysis must account for clustering. Results may not transfer to other settings, so external validity needs discussion.

sections.heading: Difference-in-differences
sections.text: Difference-in-differences compares change over time in a treated group with change in a comparison group. Suppose a clinic programme raises contraceptive uptake from 20% to 35%, while a comparison clinic rises from 25% to 30%. The estimate is (35 − 20) − (30 − 25) = 15 − 5 = 10 percentage points. This is causal only if parallel trends hold: without the programme, the groups would have changed similarly. Trends should be checked before the programme.

sections.heading: IV and propensity scores
sections.text: Instrumental variables address unmeasured confounding. An instrument Z affects treatment D but affects outcome Y only through D. The assumptions are relevance, exclusion and independence; the local average treatment effect (LATE), the effect for compliers, also needs monotonicity. Propensity scores summarise covariates: e(X) = P(D = 1 | X). Matching or weighting on e(X) balances observed covariates. It requires no unmeasured confounding and overlap. For health programmes, report assumptions and sensitivity checks.

keyPoints: Average treatment effect: ATE = E[Y(1) − Y(0)]; the counterfactual outcome is unobserved.
Randomisation makes treatment independent of potential outcomes, so groups balance in expectation.
Difference-in-differences: DiD = (Y_treated,after − Y_treated,before) − (Y_comparison,after − Y_comparison,before), valid under parallel trends.

An instrumental variable must be relevant (correlated with treatment), independent of potential outcomes (as good as random), and satisfy the exclusion restriction (affect the outcome only through treatment).
The propensity score is e(X) = P(D = 1 | X); matching or weighting needs overlap and no unmeasured confounding.
Programme evaluation should state assumptions, check balance and trends, and test sensitivity to violations.

en.title: Research Seminar and Dissertation
en.short: Planning, conducting, writing and defending a master’s dissertation in demography and social statistics.

sections.heading: Question and proposal
sections.text:
A dissertation starts with a clear question, not a broad topic. Your proposal states the problem, the gap in knowledge, the research questions, the study population, the data and a realistic timetable. It should show why the answer matters.

The literature review is not a list of summaries. It groups studies by theme, compares findings and methods, and ends with the gap your study addresses. Record every source accurately.

A master’s dissertation is modest but rigorous.

sections.heading: Design, data and ethics
sections.text:
Choose a design that can answer your question. A cross-sectional survey describes a population at one time; a cohort follows the same people over time. State your sampling method, sample size and how you will reduce non-response and measurement error. Pilot your instruments before fieldwork.

For secondary analysis, check who collected the data, for what purpose, the definitions, coverage and missing values. Write an analysis plan before you look at results.

Ethics protects participants. Seek ethics committee approval, obtain informed consent, protect confidentiality and store data securely. Do not identify individuals.

sections.heading: Analysis, writing and defence
sections.text:
Analysis should follow the plan but remain open to the data. Check data quality, describe your sample, and use methods suited to your design. For a survey estimate, report the point estimate together with its confidence interval. If you use regression, explain what each coefficient means.

Write a clear argument in a logical order: introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion and conclusion. Present tables and figures with titles and units. In the discussion, compare findings with earlier work and state limitations honestly: sample size, coverage, missing data, measurement error or design limits. Explain how limitations affect your conclusions.

Prepare an oral presentation that tells the same story in the time allowed. Rehearse, keep slides simple, and anticipate questions about your data and methods. In the defence, answer and admit what you do not know. Examiners assess your reasoning, not the size of your claims.

keyPoints: A dissertation answers one clear question and states the gap it fills.
The literature review compares and groups studies, then identifies the unresolved gap.
The design, sampling and data source must match the question and be planned before analysis.
Ethics approval, informed consent, confidentiality and secure data storage protect participants.
Report estimates with uncertainty, explain methods plainly, and state limitations honestly.
The oral defence tests your reasoning; answer directly and do not overclaim.
